coverage: Both full English editions, chapters 1-105 of 107. Named persons, named animals, and the named classical gods; the Christian God, Nature and Fortune are deliberately not cast. Peoples, places, schools of philosophy, book titles and names used as names rather than as men are not cast.

entities.name: Montaigne
entities.body: The author, who says his book and he are one thing, that he is himself the matter of it, and that he wants to be seen here in his simple, natural, ordinary fashion. He names himself rarely and late — twenty-odd times in a hundred and seven chapters — and the first occurrence of his name in either edition is not his own: it is in an editor’s note at 28:2, about the sonnets of La Boétie that the editions no longer print.

entities.name: Edward, Prince of Wales
entities.body: Edward III’s eldest son, called the Black Prince, who governed Guienne for the English crown. He stormed the city of the Limousins and would not be stopped by the cries of the people or the tears of the women and children — and then spared three French gentlemen who were holding off his whole army alone, and after them the rest of the town.

entities.name: Scanderbeg
entities.body: The prince of Epirus, famous for prodigious force and valour. Chasing one of his own soldiers to kill him, he was stopped by the man turning to face him sword in hand, and pardoned him for the resolution.

entities.name: The Emperor Conrad III
entities.body: Who besieged Guelph of Bavaria and would concede nothing but that the women in the town might walk out on foot with what they could carry — and wept for joy when they carried out their husbands, their children and the duke himself, and gave up the hatred he had conceived against him.

entities.name: Guelph, Duke of Bavaria
entities.body: Besieged by Conrad III and carried out of his own town on the shoulders of the women, whose stratagem made the emperor his friend.

entities.name: Pelopidas
entities.body: The Theban general, Epaminondas’s colleague, tried for his life with him for keeping arms past the term of their commission. He bowed under the charge, offered nothing but prayers and supplications, and was only just pardoned.

entities.name: Epaminondas
entities.body: The Theban general who broke Sparta at Leuctra, and one of the three men Montaigne names as the most excellent he knows of. Tried for his life with Pelopidas for keeping arms past the term of his commission, he answered by reciting what he had done for Thebes and reproaching his judges with ingratitude — and the court broke up rather than go on.

entities.name: Dionysius the Elder
entities.body: The tyrant of Syracuse. He took Reggio and its governor Phyton, told him his son and kindred had been drowned the day before, and had him whipped naked through the streets — and when he read in his own soldiers’ faces that they admired the man and were ready to rescue him, stopped the torture and had him drowned in private. Montaigne returns to him among the men who died of joy.

entities.name: Phyton
entities.body: The governor of Reggio, whose defence was unyielding and whose answer to the news that his son had been drowned was that they were by one day happier than he. Dragged through the streets and whipped, he declared the cause of his death aloud the whole way: that he would not surrender his country to a tyrant.

entities.name: Pompey
entities.body: Pompey the Great, who pardoned the whole city of the Mamertines, though furiously incensed at it, on the strength of one citizen’s magnanimity — and who excused himself to Posidonius for visiting him at an unseasonable hour, and got a lecture against pain for his politeness. The older edition prints his name Pompeius in that story.

entities.name: Zeno of Messina
entities.body: The citizen who took his city’s whole fault on himself and asked no favour but to be punished alone for all of them, which got the Mamertines their pardon from Pompey. Not the Zeno of the Stoics.

entities.name: Sylla
entities.body: Sulla, the Roman dictator. His host at Perugia showed the same magnanimity as Zeno of Messina and got nothing by it, for himself or for his fellow citizens.

entities.name: Alexander
entities.body: Alexander the Great, whom Montaigne calls the bravest of all men and who was reputed gracious to those he overcame — and who had Betis of Gaza’s heels bored through and the man dragged to death at a cart’s tail for refusing to speak. Montaigne asks whether valour was so familiar to him that he respected it the less, or so peculiarly his own that he could not endure it in another.

entities.name: Betis
entities.body: The commander of Gaza, found alone when the city fell, abandoned by his soldiers, his armour hacked to pieces and still fighting. He answered Alexander’s threat of every torment with a fierce and disdainful look and no word at all, and was tortured to death for the silence.

entities.name: Psammenitus
entities.body: The King of Egypt taken prisoner by Cambyses, who watched his daughter go by as a slave and his son led to execution without a word or a change of face, and broke down only at the sight of one of his own household among the captives — because, he said, that grief alone was small enough to be shown by tears.

entities.name: Cambyses
entities.body: The King of Persia who defeated and took Psammenitus, and who asked him why the ruin of his children moved him less than the misfortune of a friend.

entities.name: Iphigenia
entities.body: Agamemnon’s daughter, whose sacrifice the ancient painter painted by laying out all his art on the grief of the onlookers and then drawing her father with a veil over his face, no countenance being capable of that degree of sorrow.

entities.name: Niobe
entities.body: The mother of the poets’ story who lost seven sons and then as many daughters and was turned at last into a rock — Montaigne’s image for the dumb, deaf stupefaction of a grief too great to bear.

entities.name: Ovid
entities.body: The Latin poet of the Metamorphoses and the love poems. The older edition abbreviates the citations to “Met.”

entities.name: Ferdinand
entities.body: Who made war about Buda on the widow of King John of Hungary — the campaign in which Raisciac lost his son.

entities.name: King John of Hungary
entities.body: Whose widow Ferdinand made war on about Buda.

entities.name: Raisciac
entities.body: The German lord who had admired an unknown man-at-arms’ gallantry in the field and lamented him when he was left dead. When the armour came off he knew the body for his own son, and stood fixed on it without a word until sorrow overcame his vital spirits and he fell down dead.

entities.name: Petrarca
entities.body: The Italian poet of the sonnets to Laura.

entities.name: Lesbia
entities.body: The woman Catullus addresses, at the sight of whom, he says, his tongue grows torpid, his ears ring and his eyes are veiled in darkness.

entities.name: Catullus
entities.body: The Latin poet of the Lesbia poems.

entities.name: Seneca
entities.body: The Stoic philosopher and tragedian, Nero’s tutor. With Plutarch, one of the two writers Montaigne says he resorts to most.

entities.name: Sophocles
entities.body: The Athenian tragedian, and one of Montaigne’s examples of men who died of joy. Montaigne cannot acquiesce in the judgment of the man who, against the accusation of Sophocles’s son, concluded him capable of managing his domestic affairs from having read one of his tragedies.

entities.name: Thalna
entities.body: The Roman who died in Corsica reading the news of the honours the Senate had decreed him.

entities.name: Pope Leo X
entities.body: Who had so ardently desired the taking of Milan that the news of it threw him into a fever, of which he died.

entities.name: Diodorus the Dialectician
entities.body: Who died on the spot of shame at not being able, in his own school and before a great auditory, to disengage himself from an argument put to him. Not Diodorus Siculus the historian.

entities.name: Plato
entities.body: The Athenian philosopher, Socrates’s pupil, and with Cicero the writer Montaigne quotes most. He is an authority and an adversary in the same breath: Montaigne takes “Do thine own work, and know thyself” from him and calls a good deal of the rest of him poetry.

entities.name: Epicurus
entities.body: The Greek philosopher of pleasure rightly understood, whom Montaigne quotes often and defends against the coarse reading of him. He dispenses his sages from all foresight and care of the future.

entities.name: Livy
entities.body: The Roman historian of the city from its foundation. The older edition writes him Titus Livius at 66:0 and 73:70, and misprints him Titius Livius at 62:18, where the modern edition has the name right.

entities.name: Nero
entities.body: The emperor, Montaigne’s standing example of a prince whose reputation is fair game once he is dead: two of his own soldiers told him to his face why they hated him and why they had tried to kill him. He is also the perfect image of all cruelty who, brought the sentence of a condemned man to sign, cried out that he wished he had never been taught to write — and the man whose pardon Granius Silvanus and Statius Proximus would not live under.

entities.name: Aristotle
entities.body: The philosopher of the schools, whom Montaigne calls the god of scholastic learning and who, he says, will still have a hand in everything.

entities.name: Solon
entities.body: The Athenian lawgiver, and the author of the saying that no man can be called happy until he is dead — which Montaigne would rather put as that man is never happy, because never so till he is no more. With Lycurgus and Minos, one of the three whom Plato says their immortal children immortalise and deify.

entities.name: Lucretius
entities.body: The Latin poet of On the Nature of Things, quoted throughout the Essays.

entities.name: Bertrand de Guesclin
entities.body: The French general who died at the siege of the Castle of Rancon, and on whose corpse the besieged were made to lay down the keys of the place when they surrendered.

entities.name: Bartolommeo d’Alviano
entities.body: The Venetian general who died in the Republic’s service at Brescia, and whose body had to be carried home through enemy territory.

entities.name: Theodoro Trivulzio
entities.body: Who would not have safe-conduct asked of the Veronese for Alviano’s corpse, saying it was not fit that a man never afraid of his enemies in life should seem to fear them dead. Not the Alessandro Trivulcio killed at Reggio.

entities.name: Nicias
entities.body: The Athenian commander who lost the advantage he had visibly won over the Corinthians by suing for his dead — which under Greek law was to renounce the victory.

entities.name: Agesilaus
entities.body: The Spartan king, one of Montaigne’s standing examples of plain living and hard command — into a decrepit old age he wore the same clothes in winter that he wore in summer, and he fought obscurely armed, without imperial distinction. In the bloody battle against the Boeotians, the sharpest Xenophon says he ever saw, he waived the advantage fortune offered him of letting their battalions pass and charging the rear, judging that an effect of conduct rather than valour; he charged the front instead, was well beaten and well wounded for it, and was constrained at last to take the course he had neglected.

entities.name: Edward I, King of England
entities.body: Who had found in his long wars with Robert of Scotland that his own presence decided everything, and made his son swear to boil his body, bury the flesh, and carry the bones with the army whenever it marched against the Scots.

entities.name: Robert, King of Scotland
entities.body: Edward I’s adversary in the long wars between England and Scotland.

entities.name: John Zisca
entities.body: The Bohemian captain who fought for Wycliffe’s doctrines and left orders that they should flay him after death and make a drum of his skin to carry against his enemies.

entities.name: Wycliffe
entities.body: The English reformer whose heresies, in Montaigne’s phrase, John Zisca took up arms to vindicate.

entities.name: Captain Bayard
entities.body: Mortally wounded by a harquebuss shot and urged to retire, he answered that he would not begin at the last gasp to turn his back on the enemy, and had himself set down at the foot of a tree with his face to them. Montaigne asks in the chapter on names who would believe that Captain Bayard should have no honour but what he derives from the deeds of Peter Terrail — the two names being one man.

entities.name: The Emperor Maximilian
entities.body: A prince of great qualities and singular beauty of person, and so modest about his body that he would let nobody see him at the close-stool, and gave orders in his will that they should put drawers on him as soon as he was dead. Great-grandfather to King Philip of Spain, and father to Don Philip.

entities.name: King Philip
entities.body: Philip of Spain, reigning as Montaigne writes, and Maximilian’s great-grandson.

entities.name: Cyrus
entities.body: The founder of the Persian empire, who charged his children that neither they nor anyone else should see or touch his body once the soul had left it — a superstition, Montaigne thinks, of a piece with the reverence for religion that marks his whole life and his historian’s. Montaigne also grants that agriculture was an honour to him, as a commendation that suited his condition.

entities.name: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus
entities.body: Who forbade his heirs to spend on his hearse even the ceremonies customary at a funeral.

entities.name: Lycon
entities.body: The philosopher who told his friends to put his body where they thought fit and to make his funeral neither too superfluous nor too mean.

entities.name: Socrates
entities.body: The Athenian whose life and death Montaigne treats as the model of a human measure kept without system and without pretension. He wrote nothing; he reaches the Essays through Plato and Xenophon.

entities.name: Crito
entities.body: Socrates’s friend, who asked him at his death how he wished to be buried.

entities.name: Diomedon
entities.body: One of the Athenian captains condemned after the victory at the Arginusae for not staying to bury their dead. Allowed to speak at last, he said nothing of his own cause or of the cruelty of the sentence, but asked the gods to turn it to his judges’ good and prayed that their neglect of the vows he and his companions had made might not be visited on the city; and went to his death.

entities.name: Chabrias
entities.body: The Athenian captain-general who, beating Pollis of Sparta at Naxos, threw away the whole fruit of the victory rather than risk Diomedon’s fate, and stopped to pick up a few floating bodies while a world of living enemies sailed away.

entities.name: Pollis
entities.body: The Spartan admiral beaten by Chabrias off the Isle of Naxos.

entities.name: Ennius
entities.body: The early Latin poet, who reaches the Essays almost entirely through Cicero’s quotations of him.

entities.name: Cicero
entities.body: The Roman orator and philosopher, the most quoted writer in the Essays. Montaigne borrows his Latin constantly and thinks little of him as a man; he gives his reasons in “A consideration upon Cicero.”

entities.name: Lucan
entities.body: The Latin poet of the Pharsalia, on the civil war between Caesar and Pompey.

entities.name: Plutarch
entities.body: The Greek biographer and moralist, and the book Montaigne says he always has at hand. Most of the ancient examples in the Essays come through him, and Montaigne defends him by name against the charge of credulity.

entities.name: Bion
entities.body: The philosopher of the ready retort — it is he who asked of a king tearing his hair out for sorrow whether the man thought baldness a remedy for grief.

entities.name: Xerxes
entities.body: The Persian king who invaded Greece, and who whipped the sea and sent a written challenge to Mount Athos. Boges kept Eion for him, and would not survive the loss of it.

entities.name: Caligula
entities.body: The emperor, Montaigne’s example of a fury that destroys a thing for what happened in it: he demolished a very beautiful palace because his mother had once been happy there. It is he who condemned Julius Canus to die, and whom Montaigne calls a worthless fellow for it.

entities.name: Augustus
entities.body: The first Roman emperor, Julius Caesar’s heir. Among Montaigne’s examples of him: he defied Neptune after a storm at sea and had the god’s statue taken down from among the deities at the games, and after losing the legions under Quintilius Varus in Germany he ran his head against the wall crying “O Varus! give me back my legions!”

entities.name: Neptune
entities.body: The sea-god whose statue Augustus deposed from among the deities in revenge for a storm.

entities.name: Quintilius Varus
entities.body: The commander under whom Augustus lost his legions in Germany, running his head against the wall and crying O Varus, give me back my legions; and under whom, at 95:4, Arminius had defeated the Romans so ignominiously.

entities.name: Quintus Marcius
entities.body: The Roman legate against Perseus of Macedon, who opened sham overtures of accommodation to gain time to reinforce, and was condemned for it by the elder senators as degenerating from the Roman practice of fighting by valour and not by artifice.

entities.name: Perseus, King of Macedon
entities.body: Lulled asleep by Quintus Marcius’s overtures into granting a truce, and so giving his enemy the leisure to recruit that ruined him in the end. A prisoner at Rome afterwards, he was killed by being kept from sleep — which is why Montaigne turns to the physicians to ask whether our lives depend upon it.

entities.name: Pyrrhus
entities.body: The King of Epirus, to whom the Romans handed back his own treacherous physician rather than win by fraud.

entities.name: Polybius
entities.body: The Greek historian of Rome’s rise, cited for the Achaeans, who counted no victory won unless the enemy’s courage was fairly subdued.

entities.name: Lysander
entities.body: The Spartan admiral, whose maxim Montaigne quotes for his own countrymen: where the lion’s skin is too short, eke it out with a piece of the fox’s.

entities.name: The Seigneur de Montmord
entities.body: Who with de l’Assigni defended Mousson against the Count of Nassau, and was highly censured for going out to parley.

entities.name: The Seigneur de l’Assigni
entities.body: Montmord’s fellow defender of Mousson, censured with him.

entities.name: The Count of Nassau
entities.body: Who besieged Mousson, which the Seigneurs de Montmord and de l’Assigni were highly censured for going out of to parley with him.

entities.name: Count Guido di Rangone
entities.body: Who went out to parley at Reggio but stepped so little from his fort that when the parley fell into disorder it was l’Escut’s party, not his, that was the weaker — if Du Bellay is to be believed, for Guicciardini says he did it himself.

entities.name: The Seigneur de l’Escut
entities.body: Who came up to parley at Reggio and found himself the weaker when the parley broke down, and relied on Rangone’s honour to get him within the walls.

entities.name: Martin du Bellay
entities.body: The soldier and memoirist whose account of the French wars Montaigne uses and sometimes doubts. Not the Cardinal du Bellay, nor the poet.

entities.name: Guicciardini
entities.body: The Florentine historian, who tells the Reggio story against Du Bellay’s version.

entities.name: Alessandro Trivulcio
entities.body: Killed in the disorder at the Reggio parley. Not Theodoro Trivulzio.

entities.name: Eumenes
entities.body: The Greek secretary and general of Alexander’s successors, shut up in Nora by Antigonus. Summoned out on the ground that Antigonus was the greater man, he answered that he would never think any man greater than himself while he had his sword in his hand.

entities.name: Antigonus
entities.body: Who besieged Eumenes in Nora and had to give up his nephew Ptolomeus in hostage before Eumenes would come out to him.

entities.name: Ptolomeus
entities.body: Antigonus’s nephew, given to Eumenes as a hostage.

entities.name: Henry de Vaux
entities.body: The cavalier of Champagne besieged in the Castle of Commercy, who went out on the word of his enemy, was shown the mine that would have buried him, and thought himself so obliged that he surrendered himself and his garrison.

entities.name: Bartholomew de Brunes
entities.body: Who commanded the siege of Commercy, sapped the castle to the props, and called Henry de Vaux out to show him what waited for him.

entities.name: Lucius Aemilius Regillus
entities.body: The Roman praetor who, unable to take Phocaea by force, received the town as a confederate with every assurance of peace — and then brought his whole army in for the pomp of it and could not stop them sacking it before his face.

entities.name: Cleomenes
entities.body: The Spartan king who held that any mischief done an enemy in war was above justice, and who, having made a seven days’ truce with Argos, fell on the Argives asleep on the third night on the ground that nights had not been mentioned.

entities.name: Xenophon
entities.body: Socrates’s disciple and a soldier — both a great captain and a philosopher of the first form, as Montaigne puts it. His licence about stratagems in war is more than Montaigne will follow.

entities.name: Monsieur d’Aubigny
entities.body: Who was battering Capua when his soldiers, slack in their guard during a parley, let the French into the place unawares.

entities.name: Signor Fabricio Colonna
entities.body: Governor of Capua, who began to parley from a bastion and lost the town while he was doing it.

entities.name: Signor Juliano Romero
entities.body: Who played the novice at Yvoy by going out to parley with the Constable, and came back to find his place taken.

entities.name: The Marquess of Pescara
entities.body: Who besieged Genoa and took it by the Spaniards slipping in while the articles were as good as concluded.

entities.name: Duke Ottaviano Fregosa
entities.body: Who commanded Genoa under French protection and lost it in the middle of a treaty.

entities.name: The Count de Brienne
entities.body: Who commanded at Ligny in Barrois when the emperor beleaguered it in person.

entities.name: Bertheville
entities.body: Brienne’s lieutenant, who went out to parley at Ligny and lost the town while he was capitulating.

entities.name: Ariosto
entities.body: The Italian poet of the Orlando Furioso, quoted for the line that victory is ever worthy of praise whether won by fortune or by wit, and again for the hunter who cares nothing for the hare once he sees it taken. The older edition prints his name Aristo in the second citation — which is also the name of a Stoic and of a tragedian in this book.

entities.name: Chrysippus
entities.body: The Stoic philosopher who held that a runner should use every force he has, but may not lay a hand on his adversary to stop him or set a leg before him to throw him down. Montaigne agrees.

entities.name: Polypercon
entities.body: Who urged Alexander to use the cover of night against Darius, and was told that it was not for such a man as he to steal a victory.

entities.name: Darius
entities.body: The Persian king Alexander refused to attack by night.

entities.name: Henry VII, King of England
entities.body: Who got the Duke of Suffolk delivered into his hands on condition that he attempt nothing against the man’s life, and then commanded his son in his will to put him to death as soon as he himself was dead. Montaigne will not allow that death excused the broken faith.

entities.name: Don Philip
entities.body: Maximilian’s son and the Emperor Charles V’s father, who gave up the Duke of Suffolk to Henry VII on condition that his life be spared.

entities.name: The Emperor Charles V
entities.body: Don Philip’s son, named here to place his father more honourably.

entities.name: The Duke of Suffolk of the White Rose
entities.body: Henry VII’s enemy, who had fled to the Low Countries and was handed over on a promise that his life would be spared.

entities.name: The Duke of Alva
entities.body: Who staged the executions of the Counts Horn and Egmont at Brussels.

entities.name: Count Egmont
entities.body: On whose word and faith Count Horn had surrendered himself to the Duke of Alva, and who begged to mount the scaffold first so that death might discharge him of the obligation. Montaigne’s verdict is that death did not acquit him and that he was already discharged without dying, since no man can be bound beyond what he is able to perform.

entities.name: Count Horn
entities.body: Who surrendered himself to the Duke of Alva on Count Egmont’s security, and was executed with him at Brussels.

entities.name: Herodotus
entities.body: The Greek historian, the earliest of Montaigne’s sources for Egypt, Persia and the customs of distant nations.

entities.name: Horace
entities.body: The Latin poet of the Odes and the Art of Poetry, and the verse Montaigne quotes most often. The older edition abbreviates the citations to “Hor.”

entities.name: Martial
entities.body: The Latin epigrammatist.

entities.name: Pliny
entities.body: Pliny the Elder of the Natural History, cited for the saying that a foreigner cannot supply us the place of a man. Not the younger Pliny of the letters.

entities.name: Darius
entities.body: The Persian king who kept a prompter for his injuries: so often as he sat down to dinner, a page was to say three times in his ear, “Sir, remember the Athenians.”

entities.name: King Francis
entities.body: Francis I of France, a prince, Montaigne says, of so delicate a nostril that he caught Francesco Taverna out in a single question, and who was still keeping a secret agent in Milan when Merveille was beheaded there.

entities.name: Francesco Taverna
entities.body: Ambassador of the Duke of Milan and famous in his day for his science in talking, sent to excuse his master over Merveille’s execution. Asked by King Francis why then the thing had been done at night and as it were by stealth, he answered that the Duke would have been loth, out of respect to his Majesty, to have it done by day — and was, Montaigne guesses, well rated for it when he got home.

entities.name: Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan
entities.body: Taverna’s master, who depended on the Emperor and could not own any dealing with France.

entities.name: Merveille
entities.body: The Milanese gentleman and equerry to King Francis, sent to Milan as an ambassador in all but name and beheaded in prison at night on a pretence of murder, once the Emperor had got wind of what he was really doing there.

entities.name: Pope Julius II
entities.body: Who sent an ambassador to the King of England to set him against King Francis — and whose ambassador argued himself out of his own errand by agreeing that the war would be hard to mount.

entities.name: La Brebis
entities.body: The poet whose sonnet supplies the line that all graces were never yet given to any one man. The note gives no more than the name.

entities.name: Pope Clement
entities.body: Who at the interview with King Francis at Marseilles sent word of the argument he thought suitable, and so wasted the harangue Poyet had been preparing since Paris.

entities.name: Monsieur Poyet
entities.body: A man bred all his life at the bar and in the highest repute for eloquence, who had his speech to the Pope ready made and carried from Paris — and, the subject being changed on the day, could not contrive another.

entities.name: Cardinal du Bellay
entities.body: Who had to make the harangue to the Pope at Marseilles when Poyet could not. Not Martin du Bellay the memoirist, nor the poet.

entities.name: Severus Cassius
entities.body: Who spoke best extempore and owed more to fortune than to diligence: it was an advantage to him to be interrupted, and his adversaries were afraid to nettle him for fear his anger should redouble his eloquence. He is also the intimate friend who, seeing Labienus’s books burned, cried out that they would have to burn him too, since he carried them by heart. The older edition prints his name both ways round, Severus Cassius at 10:4 and Cassius Severus at 65:39.

entities.name: Jesus Christ
entities.body: Whose coming Montaigne uses to date the decay of the oracles, and whose thirty-three years he sets beside Alexander’s as the measure of a life that was long enough.

entities.name: Pacuvius
entities.body: The early Latin tragedian, quoted through Cicero for the wisest word in the chapter: as for those who understand the language of birds, I had rather hear them than attend to them.

entities.name: Francesco, Marquis of Saluzzo
entities.body: Lieutenant to Francis I in the army beyond the mountains, holding the marquisate by the king’s gift, with no provocation to turn and his own affection against it — and frightened into revolt, it was said, by the prognostics that everyone was spreading in Charles V’s favour. Montaigne notes that with towns and troops in his hands he could have done far more harm than he did.

entities.name: Antonio de Leyva
entities.body: Whose army lay close by Saluzzo when he revolted.

entities.name: Tages
entities.body: The demigod who rose out of a furrow with an infant’s face and an old man’s wisdom, and dictated the principles of Tuscan divination to the people who came running to look at him. Montaigne says the birth suits the art.

entities.name: Diogenes the Atheist
entities.body: Shown, in the temple at Samothrace, the offerings and painted stories of men saved from shipwreck by the gods’ especial favour, he answered that the pictures of those who were cast away are not here, and they are by much the greater number.

entities.name: Xenophanes of Colophon
entities.body: The only philosopher who acknowledged a deity and still tried to root out divination altogether — as Cicero observes, and Montaigne with him.

entities.name: Joachim the Calabrian Abbot
entities.body: Whose book, Montaigne says he would have given anything to see, foretold all the future popes with their names and qualities.

entities.name: The Emperor Leo
entities.body: Whose book prophesied all the emperors and patriarchs of Greece. Not Pope Leo X.

entities.name: Laches
entities.body: Who defined fortitude in Plato as standing firm in the ranks, and was laughed out of it by Socrates: would it be cowardice, then, to beat the enemy by giving ground? The same man who fled beside Socrates after the rout at Delium, and whose bearing in the retreat Alcibiades sets against his friend’s steady march. The older edition writes him Lachez there.

entities.name: Homer
entities.body: The poet Montaigne names among the three most excellent men the world has produced, and cites here for commending in Aeneas the science of flight.

entities.name: Aeneas
entities.body: Whose science of flight Homer commends — Socrates’s authority against Laches.

entities.name: Idanthyrses
entities.body: The Scythian king who told Darius that he did not retire out of fear but because his nation had neither fields nor cities to lose, and that if Darius wanted a battle he had only to come and look at their ancient places of sepulture.

entities.name: The Marquis de Guast
entities.body: Who went to reconnoitre Arles from behind a windmill and was spotted; the culverin was so exactly levelled at him that only his seeing the fire given and slipping aside saved him.

entities.name: The Seigneur de Bonneval
entities.body: Who with the Seneschal of Agenois saw Guast from the theatre and pointed him out.

entities.name: The Sieur de Villiers
entities.body: Commissary of the artillery, who levelled the culverin at Guast.

entities.name: Lorenzo de’ Medici, Duke of Urbino
entities.body: The queen-mother’s father, who at the siege of Mondolfo saw the cannoneer give fire at him and ducked, and was only grazed on the top of the head.

entities.name: Virgil
entities.body: The Latin poet of the Aeneid, the Georgics and the Eclogues. The citations run under the poem’s name as often as his own, spelled AEneid in the older edition and Aeneid in the modern.

entities.name: Queen Margaret of Navarre
entities.body: Who held that a gentleman is rude to go out and meet a visitor, and that it is more civil to stay at home and receive him at the door.

entities.name: The Constable Monsieur de Montmorenci
entities.body: General of the army at Dreux, where he was racked through and through with the enemy’s artillery, his battalion routed and himself taken prisoner, while the Duc de Guise halted with the forces he commanded; and who at the siege of Pavia hanged every man in the tower that had held up his crossing of the Ticino, and later trussed up the governor and ensign of the Castle of Villano for the same reason — the custom Montaigne is explaining, that a place not tenable by the rules of war may be defended only at the defenders’ own risk.

entities.name: Monsieur de Vervins
entities.body: Sentenced to death for surrendering Boulogne to the English — the case that prompted a great captain to maintain, at table, that no soldier can justly be put to death for want of courage.

entities.name: Charondas
entities.body: The legislator who, Montaigne says, brought in ignominy instead of death for cowardice: before him Greek law killed the man who fled a battle, and he ordained instead that he be exposed three days in public in woman’s clothes, in hope of getting some service out of him afterwards.

entities.name: Tertullian
entities.body: Quoted from the Apologetics for the maxim behind Charondas’s law: rather bring the blood into a man’s cheek than let it out of his body.

entities.name: Ammianus Marcellinus
entities.body: The historian, who says the Emperor Julian had ten soldiers that turned their backs against the Parthians first degraded and then put to death, and who observes the manner of the Parthians’ arming so curiously because it was so different from the Roman. Not the Tullius Marcellinus of chapter 70.

entities.name: The Emperor Julian
entities.body: Who put ten of his own soldiers to death for flight according to the ancient laws, and elsewhere, for the same offence, only sent men to live among the prisoners under the baggage ensign. Applauded one day by his courtiers for his exact justice, he said he should be proud of the praise if it came from persons that durst condemn or disapprove the contrary in case he did it.

entities.name: Cnaeus Fulvius
entities.body: Whose men ran away at his defeat and were punished, like those who fled at Cannae, with something short of death. The older edition prints him Aeneius Fulvius.

entities.name: The Seigneur de Frauget
entities.body: Lieutenant to the Mareschal de Chatillon’s company and put in command of Fuentarabia, who surrendered it to the Spaniard and was degraded from all nobility — himself and his posterity declared ignoble, taxable and for ever incapable of bearing arms, a sentence executed at Lyons.

entities.name: The Mareschal de Chatillon
entities.body: Whose company Frauget was lieutenant of.

entities.name: The Mareschal de Chabannes
entities.body: Who put Frauget into Fuentarabia in place of Monsieur de Lude.

entities.name: Monsieur de Lude
entities.body: Whom Frauget replaced at Fuentarabia.

entities.name: The Count of Nassau
entities.body: Who entered Guise, after which all the gentlemen who had been in the town were degraded like Frauget. The Essays do not say whether he is the Count of Nassau who besieged Mousson.

entities.name: Propertius
entities.body: The Latin elegiac poet. The older edition prints him Propertious in one citation and Propertius in another.

entities.name: Archidamus
entities.body: The Spartan king who told Periander that he had given up the glory of being an excellent physician to gain the repute of a very bad poet — and who was a little surprised, Montaigne fancies, at Thucydides’s answer when he asked which was the better wrestler, Pericles or himself: that it was hard to affirm, for when he had thrown him Pericles always persuaded the spectators he had had no fall, and carried away the prize.

entities.name: Periander
entities.body: Who left an excellent physician’s reputation for a bad poet’s. The older edition prints him Pertander.

entities.name: Caesar
entities.body: Julius Caesar, whose Commentaries Montaigne reads as a soldier’s book with a vanity in it: large and ample about his bridges and engines, succinct and reserved about his own valour and generalship, because the generalship was not in doubt and the engineering was.

entities.name: Monsieur de Langey
entities.body: The historian of the French wars whose account of Charles V’s speech in the Consistory at Rome Montaigne dwells on, because the ambassadors who heard it sent home a despatch with the worst of it left out.

entities.name: The Bishop of Macon
entities.body: One of the two French ambassadors present at Charles V’s speech in the Consistory.

entities.name: Monsieur du Velly
entities.body: The other French ambassador present, and with the Bishop of Macon the one who concealed the greatest part of what the Emperor said.

entities.name: P. Crassus
entities.body: Whom the Romans reputed five times happy. Consul in Asia, he sent a Greek engineer for the greater of two ships’ masts, and had the man whipped for bringing the lesser — which was, by the rules of art, the fitter of the two. Montaigne sets discipline against the work in hand and then, at the end of the chapter, wonders whether Crassus had not invited the man’s judgment after all.

entities.name: Monsieur de Bourbon
entities.body: Who took Rome — the sack in which an ensign on guard at Borgo San Pietro ran three hundred paces the wrong way in a fright, colours on his shoulder, and had to run back through the same breach.

entities.name: Captain Giulio
entities.body: Whose ensign threw himself, colours and all, out of a porthole when St Paul was taken, and was cut to pieces for it.

entities.name: The Comte de Bures
entities.body: Who with Monsieur de Reu took St Paul from the French.

entities.name: Monsieur de Reu
entities.body: Who with the Comte de Bures took St Paul.

entities.name: Germanicus
entities.body: In one of whose encounters with the Germans two great parties were so amazed with fear that each ran to the place the other had fled from.

entities.name: The Emperor Theophilus
entities.body: Who lost a battle to the Agarenes and was so stupefied that he had no power to fly, until Manuel shook him out of it with an offer to kill him.

entities.name: Manuel
entities.body: One of Theophilus’s principal commanders, who told his stupefied emperor that it was better to lose his life than, by being taken, to lose his empire.

entities.name: Quintus Curtius
entities.body: The historian of Alexander, quoted for the line that fear dreads even the means of safety. The older edition abbreviates him Quint. Curt.

entities.name: Hannibal
entities.body: The Carthaginian general, in the first pitched battle against whom ten thousand Roman foot took fright, saw no other escape for their cowardice, and charged straight through the enemy’s great battalion — buying an ignominious flight at the price a glorious victory would have cost.

entities.name: The Consul Sempronius
entities.body: The consul commanding in the first pitched battle the Romans lost against Hannibal, where ten thousand foot took fright and, seeing no other escape for their cowardice, threw themselves headlong on the enemy’s great battalion and routed it with great slaughter.

entities.name: Croesus
entities.body: The King of Lydia, taken by Cyrus and led out to execution crying “O Solon, Solon!” — because he had found what Solon told him true to his cost: that no man can be called happy until he has been seen to pass over the last day of his life. Marching his army through the waste lands near Sardis he met an infinite number of serpents, which his horses devoured with great appetite; Herodotus calls it a prodigy of ominous portent to his affairs.

entities.name: Priam
entities.body: The King of Troy, and Agesilaus’s answer to the man who called the young King of Persia happy: neither was Priam unhappy at his years.

entities.name: Ludovico Sforza, the tenth Duke of Milan
entities.body: Whom all Italy had truckled under, and who died a prisoner at Loches — but not till he had lived ten years in captivity, which Montaigne calls the worst part of his fortune. Not Francesco Sforza.

entities.name: Laberius
entities.body: The Roman playwright whose line Montaigne gives to Fortune’s victims: I have lived longer by this one day than I should have done.

entities.name: Macrobius
entities.body: The late Latin compiler, cited for Laberius’s line.

entities.name: Scipio
entities.body: Pompey’s father-in-law, who by the manner of his dying removed the ill opinion everyone had held of him until then.

entities.name: Iphicrates
entities.body: One of the three captains Epaminondas was asked to rank — himself, Chabrias and Iphicrates. “You must first see us die,” he said.

entities.name: Xenophilus
entities.body: The musician who lived a hundred and six years in perfect and continual health — Montaigne’s example that poverty and sickness can be escaped, and death cannot.

entities.name: Tantalus
entities.body: Over whom the stone hangs for ever, in Cicero’s figure for death.

entities.name: Claudianus
entities.body: The late Latin poet, quoted for the condemned man who measures his life by the length of the road to the place of execution.

entities.name: Methuselah
entities.body: Whose years are the reason, Montaigne says, that no man is so old and decrepit that he does not think he has twenty good ones left.

entities.name: Aeschylus
entities.body: Who took care to avoid the house that was threatening to fall on him, and was killed by a tortoise dropped out of an eagle’s talons.

entities.name: Aemilius Lepidus
entities.body: Who died of a stumble at his own threshold. Not the Marcus Aemilius Lepidus who forbade his heirs to pay for his hearse.

entities.name: Aufidius
entities.body: Who died of a jostle against the door as he entered the council-chamber.

entities.name: Cornelius Gallus
entities.body: The proctor, one of the men Montaigne lists as having died between the thighs of women.

entities.name: Tigillinus
entities.body: Captain of the watch at Rome, and one of the men Montaigne lists as having died between the thighs of women.

entities.name: Ludovico
entities.body: Guido di Gonzaga’s son, one of the men Montaigne lists as having died between the thighs of women.

entities.name: Guido di Gonzaga, Marquis of Mantua
entities.body: Whose son Ludovico is one of the men Montaigne lists as having died between the thighs of women.

entities.name: Speusippus
entities.body: A Platonic philosopher, and of worse example, Montaigne says, than the rest of that list — and whom Diogenes met so blown up with an inveterate dropsy that he had to be carried, and who, weary of so languishing a state of life, not long after found a means to die.

entities.name: Bebius
entities.body: The judge who gave a case eight days’ adjournment and was himself condemned by death within them, his own stay of life expiring first.

entities.name: Caius Julius
entities.body: The physician whose own eyes death closed while he was anointing a patient’s.

entities.name: Captain St. Martin
entities.body: Montaigne’s brother, twenty-three years old and already proved in the field, who took a tennis ball a little above the right ear, felt no wound, did not even sit down — and died of an apoplexy five or six hours later.

entities.name: Paulus Aemilius
entities.body: The Roman who conquered Macedon, and who answered the prisoner king’s request not to be led in the triumph with: let him make that request to himself.

entities.name: Lycurgus
entities.body: The Spartan lawgiver, cited for putting the burying-places among the churches and the busiest parts of the city, so that the sight of bones and funerals should keep people in mind of their frail condition.

entities.name: Silius Italicus
entities.body: The Latin epic poet, quoted for the old custom of enlivening a banquet with men killing each other over the cups.

entities.name: Dicaearchus
entities.body: Who compiled a register of the deaths of men — the book Montaigne says he would write himself, except that Dicaearchus meant it for a less profitable end. The older edition prints him Dicarchus.

entities.name: Maximian
entities.body: The late Latin elegist, quoted for the line: alas, to old men what portion of life remains.

entities.name: Jupiter
entities.body: Whose strong thundering hand, in Horace’s ode, does not move a well-settled soul — and who, in the story Montaigne says Plato borrowed from some lascivious poet, had not the patience to reach the couch and forgot in the pleasure of it the resolutions he had just taken with the rest of the gods.

entities.name: Manilius
entities.body: The Latin poet of the Astronomica, quoted twice in Nature’s speech: as we are born we die, and your grandsires saw no other thing than you.

entities.name: Thales
entities.body: The most eminent of the sages, whom Nature taught that living and dying were indifferent — which is why, asked why then he did not die, he answered: because it is indifferent.

entities.name: Chiron
entities.body: Who refused to be immortal once his father Saturn, the god of time and its duration, had told him the conditions.

entities.name: Saturn
entities.body: The god of time and its duration, and Chiron’s father, who told him what immortality would cost.

entities.name: Simon Thomas
entities.body: A great physician of his time, who prescribed Montaigne’s company to a rich old man with weak lungs — that the sight of a fresh complexion and the imagination of a young man’s vigour might mend his habit of body. He forgot to add, Montaigne says, that it might make the young man’s worse.

entities.name: Gallus Vibius
entities.body: Who bent his mind so hard on finding out the essence and motions of madness that he went out of his wits and never recovered his judgment — and might brag, Montaigne says, of having become a fool by too much wisdom.

entities.name: Cippus, King of Italy
entities.body: Who watched a bullfight with delight, dreamed all night that he had horns on his head, and by the force of imagination grew them.

entities.name: Antiochus
entities.body: Who fell into a fever, inflamed with the beauty of Stratonice too deeply imprinted in his soul.

entities.name: Stratonice
entities.body: Whose beauty gave Antiochus his fever.

entities.name: Lucius Cossitius
entities.body: Whom Pliny claims to have seen turned from a woman into a man on her wedding day.

entities.name: Pontanus
entities.body: Who reports a girl turning into a boy in Italy in more recent times, as Pliny reports of Lucius Cossitius.

entities.name: Iphis
entities.body: The boy who paid the vow a girl had made, in the line Montaigne quotes for such changes.

entities.name: Mary Germain
entities.body: The man the Bishop of Soissons confirmed as Germain, whom the whole town had known as a girl called Mary until she was twenty-two. Montaigne saw him at Vitry le François, full of beard, old and unmarried; he said his male organs came out when he strained himself in a leap, and the girls of the place still have a song warning each other against taking too great strides.

entities.name: King Dagobert
entities.body: Whose scars, with St Francis’s, some attribute to the force of imagination.

entities.name: St Francis
entities.body: Whose stigmata, with King Dagobert’s scars, some attribute to imagination.

entities.name: Celsus
entities.body: Who tells of a priest whose soul would be ravished into an ecstasy that left his body a long while without sense or breath.

entities.name: St Augustine
entities.body: The Father Montaigne cites more than any other, here for the man who fell into a swoon at any doleful cry and could be pinched or burned without feeling it, and for the man who could command his rear at will.

entities.name: Jacques Pelletier
entities.body: Who lived in Montaigne’s house and gave him the graven gold plate against sunstroke that Montaigne then used, with some private instructions and his own nightgown, to cure a bridegroom of an imagined impotence.

entities.name: Amasis, King of Egypt
entities.body: Who married the beautiful Greek Laodice, found himself quite another man with her, threatened to kill her for a witch — and after vows to Venus was divinely restored the first night after his sacrifices.

entities.name: Laodice
entities.body: The Greek virgin Amasis married and at first could not enjoy.

entities.name: Venus
entities.body: The goddess to whom Amasis made his vows, and was restored — and in whose avenues, Montaigne says in the chapter on education, the gods have planted more toil and sweat than in Minerva’s.

entities.name: Pythagoras
entities.body: The philosopher, cited here for his daughter-in-law’s saying that a woman must put off her modesty with her petticoat and put it on again with the same.

entities.name: Vives
entities.body: St Augustine’s commentator, who fortified his master’s example of the man who could command his rear with another, of a man who could break wind in tune.

entities.name: Charles, the Emperor and King of Bohemia
entities.body: To whom a girl from near Pisa was presented, rough and covered with hair all over — conceived so, her mother said, because a picture of St John the Baptist hung inside her bed-curtains.

entities.name: St John the Baptist
entities.body: Whose picture, hanging in the bed-curtains, the mother blamed for her hairy daughter.

entities.name: Jacob
entities.body: Whose sheep are Montaigne’s scriptural instance that a mother’s fancy marks what she carries.

entities.name: Sallust
entities.body: The Roman historian, whose glory Montaigne says he would not take the trouble to earn.

entities.name: Demades the Athenian
entities.body: Who condemned a fellow citizen for selling funeral necessaries at an unreasonable profit, on the ground that the profit could only come by the death of a great many people. Montaigne thinks the judgment ill grounded, since no gain whatever is made but at somebody’s expense.

entities.name: Albertus
entities.body: Who reports the maid that lived upon spiders — one of Montaigne’s instances that custom can carry the stomach anywhere.

entities.name: Pindar
entities.body: The Greek lyric poet, who calls custom the ruler of the world.

entities.name: Isocrates
entities.body: The Athenian rhetorician, who counselled his king to make his subjects’ trade free and their lawsuits expensive, and who says that defect is nearer allied to moderation than excess.

entities.name: Charlemagne
entities.body: Whom a Gascon gentleman, Montaigne’s countryman, was the first to oppose when he tried to impose Latin and imperial law on France — a thing Montaigne says he is obliged to fortune for.

entities.name: Phrynis
entities.body: The musician who added two strings to his instrument, and whose strings an ephor cut without stopping to ask whether they made better harmony: it was enough that they were new.

entities.name: Thyestes
entities.body: One of the three fables — with Oedipus and Macareus — by which, Montaigne says following Plato, the poets put a wholesome horror of incest into children’s heads.

entities.name: Oedipus
entities.body: One of the same three fables. The older edition prints him OEdipus, and Seneca’s play under the same spelling.

entities.name: Macareus
entities.body: With Thyestes and Oedipus, one of the three whose fables the poets have sung to children, and so infused into their tender brains the belief that makes incest horrible.

entities.name: Cotta
entities.body: The speaker in Cicero whose rule Montaigne adopts: in a question of religion, follow the high priests and not the philosophers.

entities.name: T. Coruncanius
entities.body: One of the three high priests Cotta says he follows rather than the Stoics.

entities.name: P. Scipio
entities.body: Another of the three high priests in Cotta’s list. Not Scipio Africanus, nor Pompey’s father-in-law.

entities.name: P. Scaevola
entities.body: The third of the three high priests. Not the Scaevola who slipped into Porsenna’s camp.

entities.name: Zeno
entities.body: The founder of the Stoa, and one of the three philosophers Cotta refuses to follow in a question of religion. Not the Zeno of Messina who took his city’s fault on himself.

entities.name: Cleanthes
entities.body: Zeno’s successor at the head of the Stoa, and the second of Cotta’s three philosophers.

entities.name: Thucydides
entities.body: The historian of the Peloponnesian war, cited for what happens to language in a civil war: the parties give the public vices new and more plausible names to excuse them. It is he who told Archidamus that when he had thrown Pericles the man always persuaded the spectators he had had no fall.

entities.name: Terence
entities.body: The Latin comic poet. The older edition abbreviates him Ter.

entities.name: Octavius
entities.body: Who with Cato is still reproached for having let his country go to the last extremity rather than relieve his fellow citizens at the expense of its laws. Keyed rather than aliased, because the Octavius of 99:181 is another man.

entities.name: Cato
entities.body: Cato of Utica, who would rather see the Republic ruined than saved by an innovation. Montaigne devotes a whole chapter to him later.

entities.name: Aratus
entities.body: Made admiral of Sparta in name, because an edict forbade choosing the same man twice — while Lysander went out as general of the navy and commanded in fact.

entities.name: Pericles
entities.body: The Athenian, who told a Spartan envoy that a law once engrossed on the tablet could not be taken away — and was advised to turn the tablet round instead, that being not forbidden. Montaigne’s instance of what rhetoric is for: thrown in the wrestling, he could still persuade the spectators he had had no fall and carry away the prize.

entities.name: Philopoemen
entities.body: Whom Plutarch commends for knowing how to command not only according to the laws but over them, when the public necessity required it. Against Machanidas he let his own archers and slingers be chased and cut in pieces before his face rather than leave his post, and charged the enemy’s foot only once their horse had gone off in the pursuit — the case Montaigne sets beside the Duc de Guise’s at Dreux; and he is one of the captains who held that rich accoutrement inflames a soldier’s courage. The older edition misprints his name Philopcemen in that second place.

entities.name: Apollo
entities.body: The god of the Delphic oracle, who told the people of Delphos, afraid of the Persians, to stir nothing of his treasure and to look to themselves — he was sufficient to look after what was his.

entities.name: Jacques Amyot
entities.body: Grand almoner of France, who told Montaigne the story of the prince who forgave the gentleman sent to murder him at the siege of Rouen. The older edition spells him Amiot.

entities.name: L. Cinna
entities.body: Pompey’s nephew, of an illustrious family, who conspired to kill Augustus at sacrifice — and was told the whole plot back to his face, place, day and company, and then given his life a second time. He was made consul afterwards, was Augustus’s great friend, and left him his whole estate.

entities.name: Livia
entities.body: Augustus’s wife, who asked whether he would take a woman’s counsel and then gave the advice that ended the conspiracies: severity has got you nothing — Lepidus followed Salvidienus, Murena Lepidus, Caepio Murena, Egnatius Caepio — now try clemency. She is also the one who was wont to say that to a virtuous woman a naked man was but a statue.

entities.name: Lepidus
entities.body: One of the conspirators in Livia’s list, punished before Cinna and followed by another. Neither the Marcus Aemilius Lepidus of 3:15 nor the Aemilius Lepidus who died of a stumble.

entities.name: Salvidienus
entities.body: The first name in Livia’s list of conspirators punished to no purpose.

entities.name: Murena
entities.body: The third name in Livia’s list of the conspirators severity had not stopped, after Salvidienus and Lepidus and before Caepio and Egnatius.

entities.name: Caepio
entities.body: The fourth name in Livia’s list of the conspirators severity had not stopped: Lepidus had followed Salvidienus, Murena Lepidus, Caepio Murena, and Egnatius Caepio.

entities.name: Egnatius
entities.body: The last name in Livia’s list of the conspirators severity had not stopped, and so her proof to Augustus that clemency was worth trying instead.

entities.name: The Paulli
entities.body: One of the great Roman houses Augustus names to Cinna as men who would never endure him. The older edition prints the family in the singular, Paulus, and the modern in the plural.

entities.name: The Fabii
entities.body: One of the great Roman houses Augustus names to Cinna as men who would never endure him. The older edition prints the name Fabius, the modern Fabii.

entities.name: The Cossii
entities.body: One of the great Roman houses Augustus names to Cinna as men who would never endure him.

entities.name: The Servilii
entities.body: The last of the four houses in Augustus’s list.

entities.name: Dion
entities.body: Warned that Callippus was watching for a chance to kill him, he would not inquire any further into it: he had rather die than live having to stand guard against his friends as well as his enemies.

entities.name: Callippus
entities.body: Who watched for the chance to kill Dion.

entities.name: Parmenio
entities.body: Whose letter warned Alexander that his physician Philip had been bribed by Darius to poison him; and who, on the morning of the furious battle against Darius, was forced to enter the sleeping king’s chamber and call him several times by name, the time to go and fight compelling him to it.

entities.name: Philip
entities.body: Alexander’s most beloved physician, accused by Parmenio of taking Darius’s money to poison him — to whom Alexander handed the letter to read and then drank the potion he had brought. Montaigne knows nothing else in that life with so much firm courage in it.

entities.name: Scipio
entities.body: Who to sound Syphax’s intentions left his army and his unsettled conquest in Spain and crossed to Africa in two small ships, into an enemy country and a barbarian king’s power, with no hostage and no security but his own courage.

entities.name: Syphax
entities.body: The African king whose intentions Scipio crossed the sea in two ships to sound.

entities.name: The Duke of Athens
entities.body: Who did a great many foolish things in setting up his tyranny over Florence, and this the most notable: told of the conspiracy by one of the conspirators, he put the informer to death at once, so that nobody should think the city disliked his government.

entities.name: Matteo di Morozzo
entities.body: The conspirator who brought the Duke of Athens the first news of the plot, and was executed for it.

entities.name: Du Bellay
entities.body: Joachim du Bellay the poet, whom Montaigne calls our famous poet and quotes for the line that of all things he hates pedantic learning. Not Martin the memoirist, nor the cardinal.

entities.name: Ulysses
entities.body: Whose miseries the grammarians inquire into, Dionysius said, while they know nothing of their own.

entities.name: Rabelais
entities.body: In whose Gargantua Montaigne found the proverb that the greatest clerks are not the wisest men, and whom he reckons with the Decameron and the Basia of Johannes Secundus among the books worth reading for amusement.

entities.name: Aulus Gellius
entities.body: The compiler of the Attic Nights, through whom Pacuvius’s line about men who jabber philosophy and do nothing reaches the Essays. The older edition prints the citation in the accusative, Gellium.

entities.name: Hercules
entities.body: From whom, the philosophers say, you might be the fiftieth descendant and still have nothing but a gift of fortune to boast of.

entities.name: Crates
entities.body: Asked how long it was necessary to philosophise, he answered: till our armies are no more commanded by fools. He is also named to place his brother Pasicles, the philosopher who laid his hand in the wrong place in petitioning a great man.

entities.name: Heraclitus
entities.body: Who resigned the royalty to his brother, and told the Ephesians who reproached him with playing with children before the temple that it was better than sitting at the helm of affairs in their company. Commiserating the human condition, he appeared always with a sorrowful look and tears in his eyes, where Democritus found the same condition ridiculous and never appeared abroad but laughing. Montaigne is clearly for the laughing humour — not because laughing is pleasanter, but because it expresses the more contempt.

entities.name: Empedocles
entities.body: Who refused the royalty the Agrigentines offered him, and who observed the discrepancy in them of giving themselves up to delights as if every day were their last and building as if they were to live for ever.

entities.name: Anaxagoras
entities.body: One of the philosophers Aristotle reports were called wise but not prudent, for not applying their study to more profitable things.

entities.name: Lucullus
entities.body: Whom letters alone, without any experience, made so great a captain — and who did not learn it, Montaigne says, in the perfunctory way we learn.

entities.name: Euripides
entities.body: The tragedian, quoted through Cicero for the line that he hates the wise man who is not wise in his own concern.

entities.name: Juvenal
entities.body: The Latin satirist.

entities.name: Persius
entities.body: The Latin satirist of the crabbed style.

entities.name: Protagoras
entities.body: The sophist who let his pupils either pay his demand or swear in the temple what they thought the teaching had been worth — a rule under which, Montaigne says, his own pedagogues would be sorely gravelled.

entities.name: Galen
entities.body: The physician the pedants know thoroughly, Montaigne says, and the patient’s disease not at all.

entities.name: Adrian Turnebus
entities.body: The one man of pure learning Montaigne exempts from the charge of pedantry, and in his opinion the greatest of the last thousand years: nothing of the pedant about him but the gown, and within, not a more polished soul upon earth. Montaigne says he put him on arguments far outside his profession and found him as quick as if he had spent his life in arms or affairs of state.

entities.name: Prometheus
entities.body: The Titan of Juvenal’s line, who framed the great natures of better clay.

entities.name: Stobaeus
entities.body: The anthologist through whom the Greek verse about learning without understanding reaches the Essays.

entities.name: Francis, Duke of Brittany
entities.body: John V’s son, who was told that Isabella of Scotland was homely bred and without learning, and answered that he liked her the better: a woman is wise enough if she can tell her husband’s shirt from his doublet.

entities.name: John V
entities.body: Duke of Brittany and father of the Francis who said he liked his bride the better for having been homely bred and without any manner of learning.

entities.name: Isabella of Scotland
entities.body: Whose want of learning recommended her to Francis of Brittany.

entities.name: Aristo of Chios
entities.body: The Stoic who said that philosophers did their hearers harm, because most of them were incapable of turning the instruction to good and would certainly turn it to ill. Not the Aristo who is a tragedian at 25:152, nor the Ariosto the older edition spells Aristo at 27:13.

entities.name: Aristippus
entities.body: The founder of the Cyrenaic school, out of whose school, Cicero says, came effeminate debauchees as cynics came out of Zeno’s.

entities.name: Astyages
entities.body: Cyrus’s grandfather in Xenophon, who asked him for an account of his last lesson and got the story of the two cassocks and the whipping.

entities.name: Mandane
entities.body: Cyrus’s mother, who in Cotton’s version of the story asks him how he would learn justice among the Medes with all his masters left behind in Persia.

entities.name: Antipater
entities.body: Who demanded fifty children of the Spartans for hostages and was told they would rather give him twice as many grown men, so much did they value the loss of their country’s education — and who, threatening them severely to bring them to a certain demand, was answered that if he threatened them with more than death they would die the more willingly.

entities.name: Hippias
entities.body: The sophist Socrates rallies for having made a great deal of money teaching school in the villages of Sicily and never a penny at Sparta — where, Socrates says, they are so stupid as to make no account of grammar or poetry and study only the genealogies of their kings and the rise and fall of states.

entities.name: Tamerlane
entities.body: One of Montaigne’s proofs that the most warlike nations are the most rude and ignorant, and the man who overthrew Bajazet in the furious battle after which Bajazet nearly escaped on an Arabian mare.

entities.name: King Charles VIII
entities.body: Who saw himself possessed of Naples and a good part of Tuscany almost without striking a blow — which the nobles about him put down to the princes of Italy having studied to be ingenious and learned rather than vigorous and warlike.

entities.name: Madame Diane de Foix, Comtesse de Gurson
entities.body: The chapter’s dedicatee, expecting a child. Montaigne had a hand in making her marriage and writes her his one particular fancy about how the boy should be brought up. The dedication prints her name in capitals.

entities.name: The Danaides
entities.body: Who eternally fill and whose vessels eternally run out — Montaigne’s figure for his own reading of Plutarch and Seneca. The modern edition spells them Danaids.

entities.name: Apollodorus
entities.body: Who said that if a man picked out of Chrysippus’s writings everything that was none of his, he would leave him nothing but blank paper. Not the Apollodorus whose heart spoke to him in the dream of being flayed and boiled.

entities.name: Capilupus
entities.body: A composer of centos Montaigne knew of, and one of the writers he exempts from the charge of stitching other men’s work into their own under their own name — because such men declare themselves for what they are.

entities.name: Lipsius
entities.body: Whose Politics Montaigne calls a learned and laborious contexture, and another honest example of the same declared borrowing.

entities.name: Cimon
entities.body: With Themistocles, one of the thousand men who very much deceived the expectation others had of them — Montaigne’s warning against reading a child’s promise too early. It is he who besieged Boges in Eion and offered him a safe return into Asia with all his wealth.

entities.name: Themistocles
entities.body: With Cimon, one of the men Montaigne names as having very much deceived the expectation others had formed of them as children — a warning against reading the promises of that tender age.

entities.name: Monsieur de Candale
entities.body: Diane de Foix’s uncle, who every day obliges the world with writings of his own.

entities.name: Arcesilaus
entities.body: Who, like Socrates before him, made his scholars speak first and then spoke to them — and whom pure wine despatched as it did Stilpo, though in his case not by design. The older edition prints him Arcesilas in the Apology.

entities.name: Dante
entities.body: Quoted for the line Montaigne makes his pupil’s rule: I love to doubt as well as to know.

entities.name: Epicharmus
entities.body: Who said it is the understanding that sees and hears, the understanding that orders and rules everything, and that all the other faculties are blind and deaf and without soul.

entities.name: Paluel
entities.body: One of the two noted dancers of Montaigne’s time who could not teach a man to cut capers by being watched — his figure for the pedants who mean to inform the understanding without setting it to work.

entities.name: Pompey
entities.body: The other of the two noted dancers. Not Pompey the Great.

entities.name: Signora Livia
entities.body: Whose petticoats are one of the things Montaigne says a young traveller ought not to come home able to describe. Not the Livia who was Augustus’s wife.

entities.name: Marcellus
entities.body: Whose death, Montaigne says, the pupil should be taught to judge rather than to locate: not so much where he died as why it was unworthy of his duty that he died there.

entities.name: La Boetie
entities.body: Étienne de La Boétie, Montaigne’s friend, whose “Voluntary Servitude” may have been prompted by a single sentence of Plutarch’s — that the people of Asia became the vassals of one man for not having been able to pronounce a single syllable, which is No. The modern edition spells him La Boétie.

entities.name: Alexandridas
entities.body: Who reproached a man for making very good but too long speeches to the Ephori: thou speakest the things thou shouldst speak, but not as thou shouldst speak them. The Essays do not identify him with the Anexandridas who was Cleomenes’s father, and spell the two names differently.

entities.name: Anaximenes
entities.body: Who asked Pythagoras what purpose there was in searching out the secrets of the stars with death or slavery continually before his eyes — the kings of Persia being at that moment preparing to invade his country; and who held that the air was God, procreate and immense, always moving. The older edition spells him Anaximines in the Apology.

entities.name: Gaza
entities.body: The grammarian whose method Montaigne sets against his own: precepts so intricate and harsh, and words so vain and lean, that there is no hold to be taken of them.

entities.name: Demetrius the grammarian
entities.body: Who found a knot of philosophers chatting in the temple at Delphos and told them that by their cheerful faces they could not be engaged in very deep discourse.

entities.name: Heracleon the Megarean
entities.body: Who answered him: it is for men puzzling over how a future tense is spelt to knit their brows; philosophical discourse always cheers those who entertain it and never makes them sad.

entities.name: Minerva
entities.body: The goddess of wisdom, set against Venus in that comparison, and one of the three to whom Plato gives the patronage of the young’s sports. Under her Greek name Pallas she is the goddess the Athenians adore, and the one who issued from her father’s head to communicate herself to the world — which the older edition misprints Balias. Draco and Solon gave out their laws under her name. She is not the Pallas of 69:302, who is a dead man.

entities.name: Bradamante
entities.body: One of the two mistresses Montaigne would have the tutor hold up to the boy: a natural, active, generous, manly beauty in a glittering helmet, against Angelica tricked up in curls and ribbons.

entities.name: Angelica
entities.body: Set against Bradamante when a tutor first shows his pupil a mistress: the soft, delicate, artificial, simpering and affected form, tricked up in curls and ribbons like a wanton minx, against the manly beauty in a glittering helmet.

entities.name: Flora
entities.body: With the Graces, one of the figures Speusippus painted his school with — and which Montaigne would paint a school with instead of birch and willow. Not the courtesan of 72:14 and 97:38, whose name she was taking until the census of the unkeyed table names ran over chapter 72.

entities.name: Demophoon
entities.body: Alexander the Great’s steward, who sweated in the shade and shivered in the sun. The modern edition spells him Demophoön.

entities.name: Callisthenes
entities.body: Who forfeited Alexander’s favour by refusing to pledge him a cup of wine — and whom, Montaigne notes, not even the philosophers justify for it.

entities.name: Alcibiades
entities.body: Whose constitution Montaigne admires with wonder: he could transform himself to any fashion without hurting his health, outdoing Persian luxury one while and Lacedaemonian austerity the next — as reformed in Sparta as he was voluptuous in Ionia.

entities.name: Carneades
entities.body: The philosopher Montaigne gives as his instance of a man brutified by an immoderate thirst after knowledge: so besotted with it that he would not find time so much as to comb his head or pare his nails.

entities.name: Quintilian
entities.body: The Roman teacher of rhetoric, cited for the observation that an imperious authority in a schoolmaster is often attended by dangerous consequences.

entities.name: Boccaccio
entities.body: Whose novels, Montaigne says, are harder to understand than the plain philosophical discourses he would put into a child’s hands.

entities.name: Meniceus
entities.body: The correspondent of the letter in which Epicurus says that neither the youngest should refuse to philosophise nor the oldest grow weary of it. The modern edition spells him Menoeceus.

entities.name: Leo, prince of the Phliasians
entities.body: Who asked Heraclides Ponticus what art or science he professed, and was told: neither art nor science, but I am a philosopher.

entities.name: Heraclides Ponticus
entities.body: Asked by Leo, prince of the Phliasians, what art or science he professed, he answered that he knew neither art nor science, but that he was a philosopher.

entities.name: Diogenes
entities.body: The Cynic, who when reproached that being ignorant he should pretend to philosophy answered that he pretended to it with so much the more reason. Not Diogenes the Atheist of 11:31.

entities.name: Hegesias
entities.body: Who asked Diogenes to read him a book, and was asked in return why, since he chose figs that were true and natural rather than painted ones, he did not choose exercises that were naturally true rather than written. His doctrine, which Montaigne sets beside Theodorus’s, was that a wise man ought to do nothing but for himself, forasmuch as he only was worthy of it.

entities.name: Zeuxidamus
entities.body: Who, asked why the Lacedaemonians did not write their rules of chivalry down for their young men to read, answered that it was to inure them to action and not amuse them with words.

entities.name: The Comte de la Rochefoucauld
entities.body: At the head of the troop of horse behind the two pedants on the road to Orleans — one of whom, asked who the gentleman was, and thinking his companion meant, answered that he was no gentleman but a grammarian, and that he himself was a logician.

entities.name: Aper
entities.body: Who demonstrates in Tacitus how easily the fine decoration of painted speech is effaced by the lustre of a simple and blunt truth.

entities.name: Tacitus
entities.body: The Roman historian, in whose dialogue Aper makes that case.

entities.name: Cleomenes, king of Sparta
entities.body: Who heard out the long and elegant oration of the ambassadors of Samos and then answered: as to the exordium I remember it not, nor the middle of your speech; and as for your conclusion, I will not do what you desire.

entities.name: Polycrates
entities.body: The tyrant the ambassadors of Samos wanted Cleomenes to make war on.

entities.name: Menander
entities.body: Who, reproved for not having begun the comedy he had promised, answered that it was made and ready, all but the verses: having contrived the subject and disposed the scenes, he took little care for the rest.

entities.name: Ronsard
entities.body: Who with Joachim du Bellay gave French poetry its reputation — since when, Montaigne says, every little dabbler swells his words as high and makes his cadences nearly as harmonious, and falls infinitely short of the rich descriptions of the one and the delicate invention of the other.

entities.name: Anacreon
entities.body: The Greek lyric poet, quoted for the line: what care I about the Pleiades or the stars of Taurus?

entities.name: Suetonius
entities.body: Who calls Julius Caesar’s style soldier-like — a judgment Montaigne repeats and says he cannot see the reason for.

entities.name: Aristophanes the grammarian
entities.body: Who was quite out, Montaigne says, in reproving Epicurus for his plain way of delivering himself and for an oratory whose whole design was to be understood.

entities.name: Nicolas Grouchy
entities.body: Who wrote De Comitiis Romanorum, and one of the domestic tutors who told Montaigne that his infant Latin was so fluent they were afraid to enter into discourse with him.

entities.name: Guillaume Guerente
entities.body: Who wrote a comment upon Aristotle, another of those tutors, and one of the three whose Latin tragedies Montaigne acted in at the College of Guienne. The modern edition spells him Guérente.

entities.name: George Buchanan
entities.body: The great Scottish poet, another of them, who told Montaigne he was about to write a treatise of education and meant to take his example from Montaigne’s own — being then tutor to the Comte de Brissac.

entities.name: Marc Antoine Muret
entities.body: Whom both France and Italy acknowledged for the best orator of his time, the fourth of those tutors.

entities.name: The Mareschal de Brissac
entities.body: On whom Buchanan was attending when Montaigne saw him again.

entities.name: The Comte de Brissac
entities.body: Buchanan’s pupil, who afterwards proved so valiant and brave a gentleman.

entities.name: The Counts of Foix
entities.body: The house Diane de Foix and her husband are both descended from, and whose writings Montaigne cites as evidence that learning runs in the family.

entities.name: The Graces
entities.body: With Flora, the figures Speusippus painted his school with.

entities.name: Plautus
entities.body: The Latin comic poet, one of the books the boy Montaigne ran through by stealth after Ovid and Terence, allured by the sweetness of the subject.

entities.name: Andreas Goveanus
entities.body: Principal of the College of Guienne, and without comparison the best man in that employment in France.

entities.name: Aristo the tragedian
entities.body: A man of good family and fortune, neither of which the profession blemished, nothing of the kind being a disparagement in Greece. Not Aristo of Chios.

entities.name: Chilo
entities.body: Who enjoined the rule Ne quid nimis — nothing too much — and who said: love him as if you were one day to hate him, and hate him as if you were one day to love him.

entities.name: Froissart
entities.body: In whom Montaigne finds the Comte de Foix knowing in Bearn, the day after it happened, the defeat of John of Castile.

entities.name: The Comte de Foix
entities.body: Who knew in Bearn the day after it happened of John of Castile’s defeat at Aljubarrota, and told Froissart the means by which he came to know it.

entities.name: John, king of Castile
entities.body: Defeated at the battle the older edition calls Jubera and the modern Aljubarrota.

entities.name: Pope Honorius
entities.body: Who performed King Philip Augustus’s public obsequies at Rome on the very day the king died at Mantes, and commanded the like throughout Italy.

entities.name: King Philip Augustus
entities.body: Who died at Mantes on the day Pope Honorius buried him at Rome. His name has to be bound whole, or the emperor Augustus takes the second half of it.

entities.name: Domitian
